source: Think Before You Ink Series - Manoj G S IPS (AIR 389, UPSC CSE 2025)
purpose: Tag bank for TheMCQApp MCQ engine to classify UPSC Prelims PYQs by the elimination logic/trick applicable, enabling trick-based practice sets, filters, and adaptive drills.
tag_schema_note: Each MCQ can carry MULTIPLE trick_tags (many questions combine 2-3 tricks) plus exactly one division per tag for grouping/filtering.

divisions.division_description: Tricks based on spotting specific words/phrasing patterns UPSC uses inside a statement (absolute words, qualifiers, hedges, ranges, exclusion phrases).

tags.name: Trap Words / Extreme Words
tags.logic: Absolute/extreme words (always, only, never, all, none, exclusively) in a statement are often (not always) a red flag since reality rarely has zero exceptions.

tags.name: Mild Words / Safe Words
tags.logic: Hedged/soft words (mostly, generally, usually, can, may, often) tend to be statistically safer/truer since they allow exceptions.

tags.name: "But Not" / "Only" / "Restricted To" — Artificial Exclusion
tags.logic: UPSC narrows an otherwise correct statement using exclusion phrases (but not, only, restricted to, applicable solely to) to falsely restrict scope.

tags.name: Binding / Non-Binding Language in International Agreements
tags.logic: Watch for statements that flip the actual binding/advisory nature of treaties, conventions, protocols, and international bodies' decisions.

tags.name: Approximate Data / Range-Based Statements
tags.logic: Statements using approximate ranges (about, nearly, more than, less than) are usually safer than statements giving a rigid exact figure.

tags.name: "Constitution Defines/Classifies/Explicitly Mentions" — Verification Flag
tags.logic: Whenever a statement claims the Constitution explicitly defines/classifies/mentions a term, verify carefully — UPSC often falsely attributes explicit constitutional status to terms that are only judicially interpreted or conventionally understood.

tags.name: Over-Specific / Pin-Pointed Statements Are Often Suspicious
tags.logic: Statements that are unusually narrow, precise, or pin-pointed (specific clause, specific exception, specific numeric condition) deserve extra scrutiny.

divisions.division_description: Tricks about HOW UPSC engineers a false statement structurally — by manufacturing, swapping, collapsing, or subtly tweaking facts rather than through word choice alone.

tags.name: Manufactured Wrong Statements
tags.logic: UPSC builds a wrong statement by combining several true fragments with one small false insertion, making the whole statement sound authentic and hard to catch.

tags.name: Swapping of Concepts / Features / Pairs
tags.logic: Two similar entities, features, functions, or pairs are swapped with each other (e.g., powers of one body attributed to another) to create a plausible-looking wrong statement.

tags.name: Two Similar-Looking Statements — One Small Tweak
tags.logic: Two statements look almost identical in structure/wording; a single small word or fact tweak makes one wrong. Requires close side-by-side reading.

tags.name: Triple-Fact Collapse
tags.logic: When a single statement bundles 3 factual claims together, do not assume all 3 are automatically correct — probability of at least one being wrong rises with each added claim.

tags.name: Multi-Claim Fragility
tags.logic: Rich, dense, academic-sounding statements packed with multiple claims look impressive but are structurally fragile — more claims give UPSC more places to hide an error.

tags.name: Reason-Glue Trap (Assertion-Reason)
tags.logic: In Statement I / Statement II (assertion-reason) questions, even if both statements are individually true, check whether Statement II actually explains/causes Statement I — the 'glue' between them is where UPSC hides the trap.

tags.name: Wrong Address Bluff
tags.logic: A true fact is deliberately misattributed to the wrong entity/location/authority/committee/article (correct fact, wrong 'address') — deceptively easy-looking but high-risk trap.

divisions.division_description: Tricks that don't depend on statement content at all, but on the structural pattern of the answer OPTIONS themselves (how many statements marked correct, presence of NOTA, outlier option, over-cautious phrasing).

tags.name: Number of Correct Statements Pattern
tags.logic: In 'how many of the above statements are correct' questions, use historical distribution patterns of UPSC's preferred counts as a secondary (not primary) tie-breaker — never as a standalone deciding factor.

tags.name: Odd-One-Out Option Trick
tags.logic: When one of the 4 answer options is structurally/thematically different from the other 3 (different category, different length, different pattern), it deserves a second look, as either the strongest or weakest candidate depending on context.

tags.name: NOTA / 'None of the Above' Is Usually a Weak Option
tags.logic: 'None of the above' / 'None of the statements is correct' type options are statistically less likely to be UPSC's intended answer versus a normal option, when genuinely stuck.

tags.name: The Weakest Link Strike
tags.logic: In multi-statement questions, actively hunt for the SINGLE weakest/most attackable claim across all statements rather than trying to verify everything — eliminating via the weakest link is more efficient than exhaustive verification.

tags.name: Default-True Bias
tags.logic: Counter-intuitive closing trick: don't default to doubting every statement. When no red flag is found after genuine scrutiny, lean toward marking it correct rather than manufacturing suspicion — over-elimination is as dangerous as under-elimination.

divisions.division_description: Domain-knowledge shortcuts that only apply within a specific subject area (History, Polity, IR, Environment, Schemes) based on how UPSC typically frames questions in that domain.

tags.name: UPSC's Favourite Themes in History
tags.logic: UPSC repeatedly favours certain History sub-themes (freedom movement personalities, socio-religious reform, art & architecture) — recognising recurring theme patterns helps triage unfamiliar History statements.

tags.name: International Organisations — Funding / Financial Power Trick
tags.logic: Claims about which body funds, finances, or has budgetary control over an international organisation/mechanism are a common false-attribution point — verify funding source claims specifically.

tags.name: Powerful Bodies Usually Retain Broad Powers
tags.logic: When a statement claims a normally powerful constitutional/governmental body (Parliament, President, Governor, SC/HC, Centre/State) 'has no power' or 'cannot act', treat it as a red flag — such bodies are usually designed with broad authority in their domain.

tags.name: Government Schemes — Broad Welfare Intent Right, Over-Specific Conditions Are the Trap
tags.logic: For government scheme questions, statements describing the scheme's broad welfare purpose/eligibility are usually correct, while narrow specific conditions (exact amount, exact deadline, exact exclusion) are the likely trap.

tags.name: Native-To Trap
tags.logic: In Environment/Ecology questions, claims that a species/plant/bird is 'native to' a specific region are a frequent false-attribution point — verify native vs. introduced/invasive status carefully.

tags.name: Powerless State / Wrong Rule-Maker Trap
tags.logic: In Polity/Federalism questions, claims that a State Government (or Centre) 'has no power to make rules' on a subject connected to its territory/domain are frequently false attributions of rule-making authority.

divisions.division_description: Tricks based on common-sense causal/logical reasoning rather than factual recall — useful when the aspirant doesn't know the fact but can reason about plausibility.

tags.name: Application / Use-Case Questions — 'If It Can Realistically Be Used, Don't Over-Eliminate'
tags.logic: For 'X can be used for Y' type statements, if the application is realistically plausible given the item's known properties, don't eliminate it just because it sounds unfamiliar — over-elimination on application questions is a common error.

tags.name: Consequence / Outcome Questions — Good Thing→Good Effects, Bad Thing→Bad Effects
tags.logic: For cause-effect/outcome statements, apply common-sense directional logic first: a generally positive input is unlikely to be framed with a negative consequence in a correct statement, and vice versa.
